claim: Information in a computer is quantified by the number of bits that can be stored and recovered.
source: Information in a computer is quantified by the number of bits that can be stored and recovered.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about information theory and computer science.

claim: There is a strong correlation between size and efficacy of a synapse.
source: The strong correlation between size and efficacy of a synapse allowed us to estimate the variability of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is used as a premise for the current study.

claim: Single axons make two or more synaptic contacts onto the same dendrites in hippocampal neuropil.
source: In an EM reconstruction of hippocampal neuropil we found single axons making two or more synaptic contacts onto the same dendrites, having shared histories of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the EM reconstruction data presented in the study.

claim: The spine heads and neck diameters of axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite are nearly identical in size.
source: The spine heads and neck diameters, but not neck lengths, of these pairs were nearly identical in size.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative analysis of the EM reconstruction data.

claim: The neck lengths of axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite are not nearly identical in size.
source: The spine heads and neck diameters, but not neck lengths, of these pairs were nearly identical in size.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative analysis of the EM reconstruction data.

claim: There is a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths.
source: We found that there is a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths, corresponding to storing 4.7 bits of information at each synapse.
evidence: This is calculated from the data using signal detection theory as described in the methods.

claim: Each synapse can store 4.7 bits of information.
source: We found that there is a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths, corresponding to storing 4.7 bits of information at each synapse.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of distinguishable synaptic strengths using information theory.

claim: The observed precision requires averaging activity over several minutes due to stochastic variability of synaptic activation.
source: Because of stochastic variability of synaptic activation the observed precision requires averaging activity over several minutes.
evidence: This is inferred from modeling of stochastic processes and presented in Table 1.

claim: Synapses in the hippocampus are involved in the formation of new declarative memories.
source: Synapses in the hippocampus are involved in the formation of new declarative memories.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about hippocampal function.

claim: Excitatory synapses on dendritic spines of hippocampal pyramidal neurons have a wide range of sizes.
source: Excitatory synapses on dendritic spines of hippocampal pyramidal neurons have a wide range of sizes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by the data in this study.

claim: Spine size, PSD area, number of AMPA receptors, area of presynaptic active zone, and number of docked vesicles are all highly correlated with each other.
source: Anatomical measurements of the spine size, the area of the postsynaptic density (PSD), the number of AMPA receptors, the area of the presynaptic active zone and the number of docked vesicles in the presynaptic terminal are all highly correlated with each other and with physiological measurements of the release probability and the efficacy of the synapse (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Lisman and Harris, 1994; Harris and Sultan, 1995; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Murthy et al., 2001; Branco et al., 2008; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Each anatomical characteristic (spine size, PSD area, etc.) is a correlate of synaptic strength.
source: Thus, each of these individual characteristics is a correlate of synaptic strength.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlations between these characteristics and synaptic efficacy.

claim: The sizes and strengths of synapses can increase or decrease according to the history of relative timing of presynaptic inputs and postsynaptic spikes.
source: The sizes and strengths of these synapses can increase or decrease according to the history of relative timing of presynaptic inputs and postsynaptic spikes (Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on spike-timing dependent plasticity.

claim: The failure rate at synapses depends inversely on the strength and size of the synapse.
source: The failure rate at synapses depends inversely on the strength, and therefore the size, of the synapse.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic physiology.

claim: Prior work suggests that pairs of spines on the same dendrite contacting the same axon are more similar in size than those from the same axon on different dendrites.
source: Prior work suggests that such pairs of spines are more similar in size than those from the same axon on different dendrites (Sorra and Harris, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Strong correlations were found between spine head area and spine head volume.
source: Strong correlations were found between (A) Spine head area and spine head volume
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with regression analysis.

claim: Strong correlations were found between PSD area and spine head volume.
source: Strong correlations were found between (B) PSD area and spine head volume
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with regression analysis.

claim: Strong correlations were found between spine head area and PSD area.
source: Strong correlations were found between (C) Spine head area and PSD area.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with regression analysis.

claim: Weak correlation was found between spine neck diameter and spine head volume.
source: (D) Weak correlation was found between spine neck diameter and spine head volume.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with regression analysis.

claim: No correlation was found between spine neck length and spine head volume.
source: No correlation was found between (E) spine neck length and spine head volume
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with regression analysis.

claim: No correlation was found between spine neck diameter and spine neck length.
source: No correlation was found between (F) spine neck diameter and spine neck length.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with regression analysis.

claim: The reconstruction contains 31,377 presynaptic vesicles.
source: (A) All 31,377 presynaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is a direct count from the reconstruction data.

claim: The reconstruction contains 24 docked vesicles in the example shown.
source: (B) En face view of the 24 docked vesicles (gray spheres) viewed through an axon (green) onto the PSD (red) of example spine (yellow).

claim: Number of docked vesicles is correlated strongly with PSD area.
source: (C) Number of docked vesicles is correlated strongly with both PSD area

claim: Number of docked vesicles is correlated strongly with spine head volume.
source: (C) Number of docked vesicles is correlated strongly with both PSD area and (D) spine head volume

claim: Number of docked vesicles is weakly correlated with neck diameter.
source: weakly with (E) neck diameter

claim: Number of docked vesicles is not correlated with spine neck length.
source: but is not correlated with (F) spine neck length.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F with regression analysis.

claim: The reconstruction analyzed 236 complete axonal boutons, each associated with one of the 287 complete spines.
source: n = 236 complete axonal boutons, each associated with one of the 287 complete spines.
evidence: This is a direct count from the reconstruction data.

source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Distributions of PSD areas are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Distributions of docked vesicles are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Distributions of spine neck volumes are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Distributions of spine neck diameters are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Distributions of spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: Distributions of (A) spine head volumes, (B) PSD areas, (C) docked vesicles, (D) spine neck volumes, (E) spine neck diameters, and (F) spine neck lengths are highly skewed with a long tail.
evidence: This is shown in the distribution plots in Figure 3.

claim: Pairs of spines on the same dendrite that received input from the same axon (axon-coupled) were of the same size and had nearly identical head volumes.
source: Pairs of spines on the same dendrite that received input from the same axon ('axon-coupled'), were of the same size and had nearly identical head volumes
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of axon-coupled pairs shown in Figure 4.

claim: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 occur between paired spine head volumes of axon-coupled same-dendrite spine pairs (slope = 0.91).
source: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 (dashed diagonal line) occur between paired (C) spine head volumes (slope = 0.91)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with regression analysis.

claim: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 occur between paired neck diameters of axon-coupled same-dendrite spine pairs (slope = 0.93).
source: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 (dashed diagonal line) occur between paired (D) neck diameters (slope = 0.93)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D with regression analysis.

claim: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 occur between paired PSD areas of axon-coupled same-dendrite spine pairs (slope = 0.74).
source: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 (dashed diagonal line) occur between paired (E) PSD areas (slope = 0.74)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with regression analysis.

claim: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 occur between paired docked vesicles of axon-coupled same-dendrite spine pairs (slope = 0.91).
source: Strong correlations with slopes near 1 (dashed diagonal line) occur between paired (F) docked vesicles (slope = 0.91)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F with regression analysis.

claim: Spine neck lengths of axon-coupled same-dendrite spine pairs do not show strong correlations with slopes near 1 (slope = 0.48).
source: but not (G) spine neck lengths (slope = 0.48).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G with regression analysis.

claim: Whole spine volumes of pairs of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite are highly correlated and significantly different from random pairs (KS test p = 0.018).
source: (A) Whole spine volumes of pairs of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite are highly correlated and significantly different from random pairs (KS test p = 0.018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with statistical testing.

claim: Correlation of neck volumes of pairs of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite are not significantly different from random pairs (KS test p = 0.74).
source: (B) Correlation of neck volumes of pairs of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite are not significantly different from random pairs (KS test p = 0.74).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with statistical testing.

claim: The CV of spine head volume is 0.083 and is constant across the range of sizes.
source: We found that spine head volumes ranged in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest while the CV of any given size was 0.083 and was constant across the range of sizes.
evidence: This is calculated from the data on axon-coupled pairs and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Spine head volumes range in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest.
source: We found that spine head volumes ranged in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest
evidence: This is observed from the distribution of spine head volumes in the data.

claim: At a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) of 1, an ideal observer can correctly detect whether a signal is higher or lower than some threshold 69% of the time.
source: Signal detection theory holds that at a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) of 1, a common detection threshold used in psychophysical experiments, an ideal observer can correctly detect whether a signal is higher or lower than some threshold 69% of the time
evidence: This is established knowledge from signal detection theory with citations provided.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the difference in spine head volumes and the size of the spine head volumes in axon-coupled pairs, which implies that paired small synapses are as precisely matched as paired large synapses.
source: There is no significant correlation, which implies that paired small synapses are as precisely matched as paired large synapses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and is an inference from the lack of correlation.

claim: The near-identical size relationship does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites.
source: This near-identical size relationship does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with lack of correlation.

claim: There is no correlation between spine head volumes of all pairs of axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (n=127).
source: (B) plot showing lack of correlation between spine head volumes of all pairs of axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (n=127).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with regression analysis.

claim: Randomly associated pairs of spine head volumes were not correlated.
source: (C) Similarly, randomly associated pairs of spine head volumes were not correlated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with regression analysis.

claim: There is no correlation between spine head volumes from randomly selected pairs of non-axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite.
source: plots show lack of correlation between spine head volumes from randomly selected pairs (n=127) of non-axon-coupled spines (E) on the same or (F) different dendrites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E with regression analysis.

claim: There is no correlation between spine head volumes from randomly selected pairs of non-axon-coupled spines on different dendrites.
source: plots show lack of correlation between spine head volumes from randomly selected pairs (n=127) of non-axon-coupled spines (E) on the same or (F) different dendrites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F with regression analysis.

claim: Proximity of astrocytic glial processes is not significantly correlated with spine head volumes of axon coupled pairs.
source: Proximity of astrocytic glial processes is not significantly correlated with spine head volumes of axon coupled pairs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with statistical testing of different glial proximity categories.

claim: The distribution of spine head volumes for spines that contain a spinule engulfed within the glial process does not differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
source: The KS p value is shown on each inset and indicates that none of these distributions differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with KS test results.

claim: The distribution of spine head volumes for spines that are surrounded by and making contact with a glial process does not differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
source: The KS p value is shown on each inset and indicates that none of these distributions differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with KS test results.

claim: The distribution of spine head volumes for spines that are proximal but not contacting a glial process does not differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
source: The KS p value is shown on each inset and indicates that none of these distributions differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E with KS test results.

claim: The distribution of spine head volumes for spines that are distant from any glial process does not differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
source: The KS p value is shown on each inset and indicates that none of these distributions differ from the distribution for the whole population of spines.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7G with KS test results.

claim: Over the factor of 60 range in spine head volumes there are 26 distinguishable intervals of spine sizes with a discrimination probability of 69% for each interval based on signal detection theory.
source: Over the factor of 60 range in spine head volumes from the data set there are 26 distinguishable intervals of spine sizes with a discrimination probability of 69% for each interval based on signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966; Schultz, 2007).
evidence: This is calculated from the data using signal detection theory as shown in Figure 8.

claim: The constant CV observed in the data set means that the intervals appear uniform in width and spacing on a logarithmic scale.
source: Note that the constant CV observed in the data set (Figure 5) means that the intervals appear uniform in width and spacing on a logarithmic scale.
evidence: This is an inference from the constant CV and is illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The constant CV represents a form of non-uniform quantization which efficiently encodes the dynamic range of synaptic strengths at constant precision.
source: This is a form of non-uniform quantization which efficiently encodes the dynamic range of synaptic strengths at constant precision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the constant CV finding in terms of information encoding.

claim: Time-window averaging smooths out fluctuations due to plasticity and other sources of variability including differences in the age of the synapses.
source: To explain the high precision observed in spine head volumes, we propose that time-window averaging smooths out fluctuations due to plasticity and other sources of variability including differences in the age of the synapses.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observed precision.

claim: For a release probability of 0.1 and presynaptic spiking rate of 1 Hz, the averaging time window is 21.8 minutes.
source: Table 1 gives averaging time windows T = n/R, where R is spiking rate of the presynaptic axon, for representative values of pr and a range of spiking rates. Release probability (pr) 0.1, Presynaptic spikes (n) 1306, Averaging time (R = 1 Hz) 21.8 min
evidence: This is calculated from the binomial model of release probability.

claim: For a release probability of 0.25 and presynaptic spiking rate of 1 Hz, the averaging time window is 9.68 minutes.
source: Table 1. Release probability (pr) 0.25, Presynaptic spikes (n) 581, Averaging time (R = 1 Hz) 9.68 min
evidence: This is calculated from the binomial model of release probability.

claim: For a release probability of 0.5 and presynaptic spiking rate of 1 Hz, the averaging time window is 2.42 minutes.
source: Table 1. Release probability (pr) 0.5, Presynaptic spikes (n) 145, Averaging time (R = 1 Hz) 2.42 min
evidence: This is calculated from the binomial model of release probability.

claim: Accounting for other known sources of variability at dendritic spines would require even longer time windows than those calculated for release probability alone.
source: Accounting for other known sources of variability at dendritic spines would require even longer time windows.
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of multiple sources of variability.

claim: Previous upper bounds on the variability of spine volume in the hippocampus underestimated the precision by including the spine neck volume.
source: Previous upper bounds on the variability of spine volume in the hippocampus, based on the whole spine volume (Sorra and Harris, 1993; O'Connor et al., 2005), underestimated the precision by including the spine neck volume (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which was not correlated between pairs of spines in our volume (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work and is supported by the data in this study.

claim: The dense reconstruction included a complete inventory of every synapse in the reconstructed volume and in this respect was unbiased.
source: Our dense reconstruction included a complete inventory of every synapse in the reconstructed volume and in this respect was unbiased.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology of the reconstruction.

claim: Additional pairs of synapses from two other rats confirmed that this finding is not confined to a single brain.
source: Additional pairs of synapses from two other rats confirmed that this finding is not confined to a single brain.
evidence: This is supported by data from additional animals.

claim: If 17 random pairs were chosen from all 287 synapses in the reconstructed volume, there is only a one in 5000 chance that the spine heads would be as precisely matched as the 17 axon-coupled pairs discovered.
source: To make this p value concrete, if 17 random pairs were chosen from all 287 synapses in the reconstructed volume, there is only a one in 5000 chance that the spine heads would be as precisely matched as the 17 axon-coupled pairs discovered here.
evidence: This is a statistical interpretation of the KS test p=0.0002.

claim: The high correlation between the PSD areas and numbers of docked vesicles observed in axon-coupled spines is not surprising given the high correlation between head sizes.
source: Since the correlations between the head sizes of axon-coupled pairs of spines is high, the high correlation between the PSD areas and numbers of docked vesicles observed in axon-coupled spines is not surprising (Figures 4E and 4F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known correlations between these features.

claim: It was unexpected to find that the spine neck diameters were highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs of spines (r2=0.70).
source: However, it was unexpected to find that the spine neck diameters were also highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs of spines (Figure 4D r2=0.70), since the correlation between spine head volumes and spine neck diameters is not statistically significant (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data that contrasts with expectations based on other correlations.

claim: There are at least two geometric aspects of the spine geometry that are under tight control of synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, there are at least two geometric aspects of the spine geometry that are under tight control of synaptic plasticity, which may reflect different aspects of synaptic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that both head volume and neck diameter are tightly controlled in axon-coupled pairs.

claim: The diameter of the spine neck may reflect the need for trafficking of materials between the spine shaft and spine head, which is known to be regulated by LTP and LTD.
source: The diameter of the spine neck may reflect the need for trafficking of materials between the spine shaft and spine head, which is known to be regulated by LTP and LTD (Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Highly correlated release probability at multiple contacts in the neocortex between the axon of a given layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron and the same target cell has been reported.
source: Complementing our observations and analysis in the hippocampus, highly correlated pr at multiple contacts in the neocortex between the axon of a given layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron and the same target cell has been reported (Koester and Johnston, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work in neocortex.

claim: The estimate of synaptic variability based on spine head volume is an order of magnitude lower than estimates based on release probability.
source: Our estimate of synaptic variability, based on spine head volume, is an order of magnitude lower.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and prior work.

claim: In a recent connectomic reconstruction of the mouse cortex, the similarity in the volumes of axon-coupled pairs of dendritic spines were statistically significant.
source: In a recent connectomic reconstruction of the mouse cortex, the similarity in the volumes of axon-coupled pairs of dendritic spines were statistically significant (Kasthuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work in mouse cortex.

claim: The observation of similar spine volumes in axon-coupled pairs is further evidence for the high precision of synaptic plasticity and suggests that the same may be true in other brain areas.
source: This observation is further evidence for the high precision of synaptic plasticity and suggests that the same may be true in other brain areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on findings in both hippocampus and cortex.

claim: Two synapses from the same axon on two different dendrites of the same neuron might not share the same postsynaptic history.
source: Related to this question, two synapses from the same axon on two different dendrites of the same neuron might not share the same postsynaptic history.
evidence: This is speculation about postsynaptic history based on dendritic compartmentalization.

claim: Synaptic tagging and capture is much less effective when the synapses are on different branches.
source: Synaptic tagging and capture, in which inputs that are too weak to trigger LTP or LTD can be 'rescued' by a stronger input to neighboring synapses if it occurs within an hour (Frey and Morris, 1997; O'Donnell and Sejnowski, 2014), is much less effective when the synapses are on different branches (Govindarajan et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on synaptic tagging and capture.

claim: The unusual triple synapse from a single axon was excluded from the analysis because the presynaptic terminal was a single large varicosity filled with vesicles (MSB) shared by three synapses.
source: An unusual triple synapse from a single axon (Figure 4B, 'k, l, m') was excluded from the analysis because the presynaptic terminal was a single large varicosity filled with vesicles (i.e. an MSB) shared by three synapses, unlike the other pairs that had isolated presynaptic specializations (n=9), or an MSB shared by two synapses (n=8).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the structural characteristics of the synapse.

claim: The estimate of variability would not be greatly affected by including the 3 additional pairs of synapses from the triple synapse in the analysis.
source: Regardless of the explanation, our estimate of the variability would not be greatly affected by including these 3 additional pairs of synapses in the analysis.
evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of the findings.

claim: One way that high precision can be achieved is through time averaging.
source: One way that high precision can be achieved is through time averaging.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observed precision.

claim: Long-term changes in the structure of the synapse and the efficacy of synaptic transmission are triggered by the entry of calcium into the spine.
source: Long-term changes in the structure of the synapse and the efficacy of synaptic transmission are triggered by the entry of calcium into the spine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Phosphorylation of CaMKII integrates calcium signals over minutes to hours and is a critical step in enzyme cascades leading to structural changes induced by LTP and LTD.
source: Phosphorylation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), required for spike-timing dependent plasticity processes, integrates calcium signals over minutes to hours and is a critical step in enzyme cascades leading to structural changes induced by long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) (Kennedy et al., 2005), including rearrangements of the cytoskeleton (Kramár et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on CaMKII function.

claim: The time window over which CaMKII integrates calcium signals is within the range of time windows predicted to be needed to achieve the observed precision.
source: The time window over which CaMKII integrates calcium signals is within the range of time windows we predict would be needed to achieve the observed precision (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the CaMKII time scale with the calculated averaging time windows.

claim: Similar time windows occur in synaptic tagging and capture, which also requires CaMKII.
source: Similar time windows occur in synaptic tagging and capture, which also requires CaMKII (Redondo and Morris, 2011; de Carvalho Myskiw et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on synaptic tagging and capture.

claim: Biochemical pathways within the postsynaptic spine have the long time scales required to record and maintain the history of activity patterns leading to structural changes in the size of the spine heads.
source: These observations suggest that biochemical pathways within the postsynaptic spine have the long time scales required to record and maintain the history of activity patterns leading to structural changes in the size of the spine heads.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time scales of CaMKII and synaptic tagging.

claim: The information stored at a single synapse is encoded in the form of the synaptic strength, which reflects the pre- and postsynaptic history experienced by the synapse.
source: The information stored at a single synapse is encoded in the form of the synaptic strength, which reflects the pre- and postsynaptic history experienced by the synapse.
evidence: This is a statement about how information is encoded at synapses.

claim: Due to the many sources of variability, the information stored at a synapse cannot be read out with a single input spike.
source: But due to the many sources of variability, this information cannot be read out with a single input spike.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stochastic nature of synaptic transmission.

claim: The stochastic variability might reflect a sampling strategy designed for energetic efficiency since it is the physical substrate that must be stable for long-term memory retention, not the read out of individual spikes.
source: First, the stochastic variability might reflect a sampling strategy designed for energetic efficiency since it is the physical substrate that must be stable for long-term memory retention, not the read out of individual spikes (Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of stochastic variability, supported by a citation.

claim: Each synapse in essence samples from a probability distribution with a highly accurate mean, which collectively produces a sample from the joint probability distribution across all synapses.
source: Each synapse in essence samples from a probability distribution with a highly accurate mean, which collectively produces a sample from the joint probability distribution across all synapses.
evidence: This is speculation about how synapses might implement probabilistic sampling.

claim: Drop out is a procedure in which only a random fraction of the elements in a model are used on any given trial, which can ameliorate the problem of overfitting.
source: This problem can be ameliorated by 'drop out', a procedure in which only a random fraction of the elements in the model are used on any given trial (Wan et al., 2013; Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from machine learning, supported by citations.

claim: Drop out regularizes the learning since a different network is being used on every learning trial, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting.
source: Drop out regularizes the learning since a different network is being used on every learning trial, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting.
evidence: This is established knowledge from machine learning about how dropout works.

claim: The upper bound on the variability found in this study may be limited by errors in the reconstruction and could be even lower if a more accurate method could be devised.
source: The upper bound on the variability that we have found may be limited by errors in the reconstruction and could be even lower if a more accurate method could be devised to compute the volume of a spine head, neck diameter, PSD area, number of docked vesicles, or other salient features of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the current methods.

claim: Much can be learned about the computational resources of synapses by exploring axon-coupled synaptic pairs in other brain regions and in other species.
source: Much can be learned about the computational resources of synapses by exploring axon-coupled synaptic pairs in other brain regions and in other species.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Images were obtained from serial thin sections in the middle of stratum radiatum of hippocampal area CA1 from three adult male rats (55–65 days old).
source: Images were obtained from serial thin sections in the middle of stratum radiatum of hippocampal area CA1 from three adult male rats (55–65 days old) (Mishchenko et al., 2010; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and data sources.

claim: One set of images was used to make a dense model of 6 x 6 x 5 μm³ of hippocampal neuropil.
source: One set of images was used to make a dense model of 6 x 6 x 5 μm3 of hippocampal neuropil and processed as previously described in a study of the extracellular space (Kinney et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the reconstruction volume.

claim: In the dense data set, 13 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 11 dendrites were identified.
source: In this data set, we identified 13 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 11 dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a count from the reconstruction data.

claim: In the other two data sets, 7 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 4 dendrites were identified for a total of 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs.
source: In this data set, we identified 7 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 4 dendrites for a total of 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs.
evidence: This is a count from the reconstruction data.

claim: A total of 449 synaptic contacts were found in the dense reconstructed volume of neuropil.
source: A total of 449 synaptic contacts were found in the dense reconstructed volume of neuropil.
evidence: This is a count from the reconstruction data.

claim: 142 synapses were excluded from the analysis because they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set.
source: We excluded a number of synapses from the analysis if they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set (142)
evidence: This is a methodological decision about data inclusion criteria.

claim: 20 shaft synapses were excluded from the analysis.
